plain_english: Let me explain, since we both agree these things are worth wanting, why I count them among good things and how I would act differently toward you if I had them. Put me in charge of a very rich man's house. Put me where gold and silver dishes are used for everyday meals. I won't think more of myself because of things that may be in my house but are not part of who I am. Take me away to the wooden bridge and set me down among the beggars. I won't despise myself for sitting with people who hold out their hands for money. What does lacking a piece of bread matter to someone who still has the power to die? So what's my point? I'd prefer the grand house to the beggar's bridge. Put me among beautiful furniture and all the tools of luxury. I won't think myself any happier because my cloak is soft or because my guests lie on purple cushions.
original_excerpt: Learn, then, since we both agree that they are desirable, what my reason is amongst counting them among good things, and in what respects I should behave differently to you if I possessed them. Place me as master in the house of a very rich man: place me where gold and silver plate is used for the commonest purposes; I shall not think more of myself because of things which even though they are in my house are yet no part of me. Take me away to the wooden bridge[5] and put me down there among the beggars: I shall not despise myself because I am sitting among those who hold out their hands for alms: for what can the lack of a piece of bread matter to one who does not lack the power of dying? Well, then? I prefer the magnificent house to the beggar's bridge.

plain_english: Picture a different scene: I won't be any more miserable if my tired head rests on a bundle of hay instead of lying on a circus cushion with all the stuffing about to burst through its worn, patched fabric. So what's my point? I'd rather show myself in public dressed in fine wool and official robes than with bare or half-covered shoulders. I'd like every day's business to go exactly as I want it to, with fresh congratulations constantly following the last ones. But I won't let this make me proud. Change all this good fortune to its opposite. Let my mind be torn apart by losses, grief, and all kinds of attacks. Let no hour pass without some argument. Even then, surrounded by the worst troubles, I won't call myself the most miserable person alive. I won't curse any particular day, because I've made sure I have no unlucky days. So what's the point of all this? I'd rather have to control my joys than suppress my sorrows.
original_excerpt: Place me among magnificent furniture and all the appliances of luxury: I shall not think myself any happier because my cloak is soft, because my guests rest upon purple. Change the scene: I shall be no more miserable if my weary head rests upon a bundle of hay, if I lie upon a cushion from the circus, with all the stuffing on the point of coming out through its patches of threadbare cloth. Well, then? I prefer, as far as my feelings go, to show myself in public dressed in woollen and in robes of office, rather than with naked or half-covered shoulders: I should like every day's business to turn out just as I wish it to do, and new congratulations to be constantly following upon the former ones: yet I will not pride myself upon this: change all this good fortune for its opposite, let my spirit be distracted by losses, grief, various kinds of attacks: let no hour pass without some dispute: I shall not on this account, though beset by the greatest miseries, call myself the most miserable of beings, nor shall I curse any particular day, for I have taken care to have no unlucky days. What, then, is the upshot of all this? it is that I prefer to have to regulate joys than to stifle sorrows.

plain_english: The great Socrates would tell you the same thing. "Make me the conqueror of all nations," he would say. "Let me ride in triumph through Thebes in Bacchus's golden chariot, from east to west. Let Persian kings take orders from me. Even then, I'll still know I'm just a man, even when everyone around me calls me a god. Now connect this great height with a sudden fall into disaster. Put me on some foreign chariot to decorate a cruel conqueror's victory parade. I'll follow behind another man's chariot with no more shame than I showed when I rode in my own. So what? Despite all this, I'd still rather be the conqueror than the prisoner. I despise Fortune's entire kingdom, but if I had to choose, I'd pick the better parts. I'll turn whatever happens to me into something good. But I'd prefer what happens to be comfortable, pleasant, and unlikely to annoy me. Don't think that virtue comes without effort — some virtues need a kick in the pants, while others need to be reined in."
original_excerpt: The great Socrates would say the same thing to you. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations: let the voluptuous car of Bacchus bear me in triumph to Thebes from the rising of the sun: let the kings of the Persians receive laws from me: yet I shall feel myself to be a man at the very moment when all around salute me as a God. Straightway connect this lofty height with a headlong fall into misfortune: let me be placed upon a foreign chariot that I may grace the triumph of a proud and savage conqueror: I will follow another's car with no more humility than I showed when I stood in my own. What then? In spite of all this, I had rather be a conqueror than a captive. I despise the whole dominion of Fortune, but still, if I were given my choice, I would choose its better parts. I shall make whatever befals me become a good thing, but I prefer that what befals me should be comfortable and pleasant and unlikely to cause me annoyance: for you need not suppose that any virtue exists without labour, but some virtues need spurs, while others need the curb."

plain_english: Just as we have to hold back our body when going downhill and push it hard when climbing up, some virtues work the same way. Some virtues lead us downhill, others uphill. Think about it — patience, courage, and persistence all have to fight strong opposition and crush bad luck underfoot. These virtues are clearly climbing, struggling, fighting their way up a steep hill. But what about generosity, moderation, and gentleness? These glide easily downhill. With the gentle virtues, we must hold back our spirit so it doesn't run away with us. With the tough virtues, we must push and drive ourselves forward. So we should use the energetic, fighting virtues when we're poor. When we're rich, we should use the gentler virtues that move lightly and just carry their own weight. Given this difference, I'd rather deal with virtues I can practice in peace than ones I can only try through blood and sweat. "This is why," says the wise man, "I don't say one thing and do another. But you don't really understand what I'm saying. You only hear the sound of my words. You don't try to figure out what they mean."
original_excerpt: As we have to check our body on a downward path, and to urge it to climb a steep one; so also the path of some virtues leads down hill, that of others uphill. Can we doubt that patience, courage, constancy, and all the other virtues which have to meet strong opposition, and to trample Fortune under their feet, are climbing, struggling, winning their way up a steep ascent? Why! is it not equally evident that generosity, moderation, and gentleness glide easily downhill? With the latter we must hold in our spirit, lest it run away with us: with the former we must urge and spur it on. We ought, therefore, to apply these energetic, combative virtues to poverty, and to riches those other more thrifty ones which trip lightly along, and merely support their own weight. This being the distinction between them, I would rather have to deal with those which I could practise in comparative quiet, than those of which one can only make trial through blood and sweat. "Wherefore," says the sage, "I do not talk one way and live another: but you do not rightly understand what I say: the sound of my words alone reaches your ears, you do not try to find out their meaning."
